The post Meet Vivian Ho: the 17-year-old who built a supply network around dignity, not charity first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under.

Most social programs ask you to declare yourself before they’ll give you anything. You fill out a form, check a box, explain your circumstances to someone with authority over the outcome. Vivian Ho built All The Same Organization around the idea that this moment, identifying yourself as someone who needs help, was what kept people from asking at all. Vivian lives in Cedar Park, Texas, but the organization operates nationally. She is, remarkably, only 17 years old.

ATS delivers supply packages directly to low-income families through Title I schools: food, hygiene products, household necessities, school supplies. Families request what they need through an anonymous sign-up system. No one who receives support is required to name themselves as the recipient.

“Just because resources exist does not mean that it’s accessible,” wrote Anika Luangaphay, who co-founded ATS alongside Vivian. The anonymous system, Luangaphay explained, was designed to let families “choose what type of support they want” without attaching their identity to the request.

Reaching Title I families across the country

Since its founding, ATS has grown to more than 200 chapters with roughly 8,000 volunteers and has distributed over 150,000 supplies to families at Title I schools. In a single back-to-school season, the organization served five schools and delivered more than 15,000 school supplies. Vendor events in the Austin and Cedar Park area have raised more than $75,000 in goods.

ATS brings supplies directly to schools, removing the need for families to travel. Outreach is conducted across language barriers so that immigrant families can find and navigate the program without information being another wall to get over.

Aoto Yamazaki, a longtime volunteer, described Vivian’s approach as incredibly empathetic and well-thought-out: “What makes Vivian’s work especially meaningful to me is how intentionally she considers each student’s culture due to her past experiences as an immigrant.”

Cultural Surprises

Cultural Surprises works like this: volunteers research the cultural background of a recipient family, then create handmade arts and crafts based on what they find. The crafts go out alongside the supply packages. More than 500 crafts have been made for over 60 recipients. Volunteers don’t just pack boxes; they do the work to understand the people they’re packing for.

Yamazaki wrote that the program had changed what he understood about volunteering: “Being part of this work has taught me so much about cultures I previously knew little about, including Hmong culture.”

Luangaphay connected it directly to Vivian’s own history. “She had told me herself that she grew up suppressing her culture due to being a Vietnamese immigrant,” Luangaphay wrote, “so now she recognizes the students in Title I schools often neglect their own culture, too.” The crafts are partly a way of giving back something that growing up between cultures tends to cost.

ATS has now secured funding for a Cultural Spotlight Scholarship. Rather than asking volunteers to make crafts for recipients, this program invites students to create art and crafts inspired by their own cultures, with a short written description of what the piece means and where it comes from. Those descriptions get shared with a wider audience. Winners will receive $1,250. The goal, as Luangaphay described it, is to give participants “a deep dive into a culture, whether it’s their own or another person’s.”

A classroom, and what came after

After noticing a gap in career exposure at the schools she worked with, Vivian fundraised for medical supplies, including mannequins, suture kits, and stethoscopes, then developed a partnership with Age of Central Texas to build a functional medical classroom at Dobie Middle School.

When the school went through a turnaround and that classroom was shut down, she turned her attention to other Title I schools rather than walking away.

“Her willingness to keep finding ways to help, even when her original efforts did not go as planned, is something that has always stayed with me,” Yamazaki wrote.

Yamazaki saw the same thing in smaller moments. Early in his time with the organization, he told Vivian he wanted to start his own project after being inspired by her work. “She selflessly gave me her time, advice, and guidance, walking me through how to turn my ideas into something that could create a real impact,” he wrote. She was, at that point, a teenager running a multi-chapter national nonprofit.

Vivian received two nominations for this series: one from her co-founder and one from a volunteer she inspired to build something of his own. Both of them described an organization built on one idea: that people should be able to ask for help without giving anything of themselves away to get it. Learn more and get involved at www.allthesame.org.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News
articles.reasoning: The article describes a 17-year-old founder creating a national nonprofit that provides anonymous, dignity-centered support to low-income families, removing barriers to access and respecting cultural identities. The organization has broad impact across many Title I schools, serving thousands of families, and includes innovative cultural and educational programs. This represents a meaningful, scalable social innovation improving access to resources and fostering inclusion.
articles.personality_title: 17-year-old Vivian Ho creates national nonprofit delivering help with dignity and respect
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many social programs require people to share personal details before getting help, which can stop some from asking for what they need. Vivian Ho, a 17-year-old in Texas, saw this problem and wanted to change it.

**What happened** – Vivian started All The Same Organization (ATS), which delivers food, school supplies, and hygiene products to low-income families without asking them to reveal their identity. Families request items anonymously through schools called Title I schools, which serve students from low-income families. ATS now has over 200 chapters, 8,000 volunteers, and has given out more than 150,000 supply packages across the country.

**Impact** – ATS makes it easier for families to get help without feeling embarrassed or judged. It also respects different cultures by including handmade crafts that reflect the families’ backgrounds. This helps families feel seen and valued. Vivian’s work also inspired volunteers to learn about new cultures and helped start a scholarship program encouraging students to share their own culture through art.

**What's next step** – ATS will continue growing its network and programs, including the Cultural Spotlight Scholarship that gives money to students who create art about their culture. Vivian and her team plan to keep finding new ways to support families and make sure help is easy to access for everyone.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Vivian Ho’s nonprofit shows how helping people with respect and privacy can reach thousands and celebrate diverse cultures at the same time.

articles.title: For Indigenous peoples in Brazil, the election results offer a reprieve — not a resolution
articles.content:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection as president of Brazil gave Indigenous communities a measure of relief after a campaign in which his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, promised to halt recognition of new Indigenous territories and push for more mining and development.

“For Indigenous Peoples, the reelection of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is more than a victory, and it is bigger than Brazil,” said Edson Krenak, who is Indigenous Krenak. “It is not about victory; it is about the possibility to dream and to fight without fear of death.”

But Sunday’s runoff election strengthened Bolsonaro’s movement in Congress, where his Liberal Party won the largest number of seats in both houses and the broader right gained a Senate majority. Leaders warn that this could open their territories to mining, weaken environmental protections, and roll back land rights, making it much harder for Lula to advance his Indigenous and environmental agendas.

Climate Observatory, a nonprofit coalition of 172 organizations, says 70 percent of the incoming lawmakers oppose the climate and environmental agenda, according to The Associated Press.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The stakes were especially high for Indigenous peoples because Bolsonaro campaigned on policies aligned with those of his father Jair Bolsonaro, whose presidency from 2019 to 2023 saw an increase in mining, land grabs, deforestation, and attacks on their rights. Amazon deforestation reached a record in 2022, and Indigenous leaders say their communities endured unchecked violence from illegal mining operations during the elder Bolsonaro’s time in office.

His son finished more than 2 million votes ahead of Lula in the first election earlier this month, but neither candidate secured the 50 percent required to win outright. That result sparked fear in Indigenous communities and environmental advocates, who warned that the future of the Amazon was at stake. Lula came back to win Sunday’s runoff by roughly 4.4 million votes, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive term as president.

In an interview between the two rounds of voting, Toya Manchineri, the general coordinator of the Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon, or COIAB, said Indigenous peoples across the rainforest were deeply concerned about the possibility of a Bolsonaro win. Much of the last three years of Lula’s administration were spent undoing the damage the Bolsonaro administration caused, Manchineri said.

Manchineri said Lula’s term has largely been a period of rebuilding as Indigenous peoples gained greater roles in decision making. “We were only beginning to see the resources returning,” he said.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

In 2023, the administration established the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples and appointed Sônia Guajajara to lead it. Lula also revitalized the federal Indigenous affairs agency FUNAI after Bolsonaro had used it to support agribusiness, despite Indigenous resistance. The government also announced just before the election that Amazon deforestation had fallen to its lowest level since recordkeeping began in 1988, according to the AP.

Still, Indigenous leaders say the progress made under Lula has not resolved deeper conflicts over land, development, and decision-making.

“Lula’s victory prevents a president who promised to halt Indigenous land demarcation from taking office, but our territories are far from safe,” Alessandra Korap Munduruku, coordinator of the Munduruku Pariri Indigenous Association, said in a statement. “We have demanded that Lula’s government respect our decisions and listen to Indigenous Peoples before advancing projects that affect our rivers and forests. Congress has become more dangerous for us, and we must remain organized. Our struggle does not end with an election’s outcome.”

For Indigenous organizations, Lula’s victory is cause for hope, but they must now work with a Congress dominated by lawmakers who have already voted in favor of easing environmental protections and against Indigenous land claims. Given that dynamic, Krenak expressed concern about the difficulty Lula may face advancing his agenda. “The costs of negotiating with the Congress and senate will be very high, if ever successful,” he said.

The election also came amid years of Indigenous voters struggling to access the polls. Earlier this month, a court denied a request for transportation assistance filed by Indigenous peoples in the Javari Valley in northern Brazil. Other efforts were more successful: Court rulings elsewhere helped secure government transportation for Indigenous voters in remote areas, while Indigenous communities across the Amazon organized to increase turnout, AP reported.

“Despite the challenges faced throughout the electoral process, Indigenous peoples of the Amazon made their voices heard at the polls across all nine states of the Brazilian Amazon, reaffirming their commitment to democracy, national sovereignty, and the defense of Indigenous rights. We marked the ballot boxes in defense of life, our territories, and Brazil’s future!” COIAB said in a statement. “Brazil’s future is Indigenous, and it begins in our territories! WE ARE THE ANSWER!”

For Krenak, however, Lula’s victory is only the beginning. He says he wants to see more meaningful progress during the president’s next term.

“By 2030, success should not be measured by how many Indigenous leaders stand besides officials at summits,” he said. “But by whether Indigenous Peoples gain real authority to prevent their territories to become sacrifice zones, but territories of life, reciprocity and generosity.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the reelection of Brazil's president Lula, which Indigenous peoples see as a hopeful reprieve from policies threatening their land and rights. It highlights meaningful political progress, Indigenous participation, and environmental protection efforts, with broad societal implications for Indigenous rights and Amazon conservation. Despite challenges ahead, the story focuses on tangible political and social advancements for Indigenous communities, making it an inspiring and significant human rights development.
articles.personality_title: Lula’s reelection brings cautious hope for Brazil’s Indigenous communities
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Brazil’s Indigenous peoples have faced growing threats to their land and rights in recent years, especially during the presidency of Jair Bolsonaro from 2019 to 2023. His government allowed more mining and deforestation in the Amazon and weakened protections for Indigenous territories.

**What happened** – Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected president of Brazil in a runoff vote in October 2022. Indigenous leaders welcomed his victory as a chance to protect their lands and rights after a tough campaign where his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, promised to stop recognizing new Indigenous territories and increase mining.

**Impact** – Lula’s return has helped rebuild government support for Indigenous peoples. His administration created a Ministry of Indigenous Peoples and strengthened the federal agency that protects Indigenous land. They also announced the lowest Amazon deforestation rate since 1988. However, the new Congress has many lawmakers who oppose Indigenous land rights and environmental protections, making progress uncertain.

**What's next step** – Indigenous leaders say they must stay organized and push the government to respect their decisions. Lula will need to negotiate carefully with a Congress that may resist his environmental and Indigenous policies. Indigenous communities also continue working to improve voting access and make their voices heard in Brazil’s democracy.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Lula’s reelection offers Brazil’s Indigenous peoples a vital chance to protect their lands and rights, but real progress depends on overcoming political challenges ahead.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a été réélu président du Brésil lors d’un second tour en octobre 2022. Les leaders autochtones ont accueilli sa victoire comme une chance de protéger leurs terres et droits après une campagne difficile où son adversaire, Flávio Bolsonaro, avait promis d’arrêter de reconnaître de nouveaux territoires autochtones et d’augmenter l’exploitation minière.

**Impact** – Le retour de Lula a permis de reconstruire le soutien gouvernemental aux peuples autochtones. Son administration a créé un ministère des Peuples autochtones et renforcé l’agence fédérale qui protège les terres autochtones. Ils ont aussi annoncé le taux de déforestation le plus bas en Amazonie depuis 1988. Cependant, le nouveau Congrès compte beaucoup de députés opposés aux droits fonciers autochtones et aux protections environnementales, ce qui rend le progrès incertain.

**Message en une phrase** – La réélection de Lula offre aux peuples autochtones du Brésil une chance essentielle de protéger leurs terres et droits, mais de vrais progrès dépendent des défis politiques à venir.
articles.personality_title_es: La reelección de Lula trae una esperanza cautelosa para los pueblos indígenas de Brasil
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los pueblos indígenas de Brasil han enfrentado crecientes amenazas a sus tierras y derechos en los últimos años, especialmente durante la presidencia de Jair Bolsonaro de 2019 a 2023. Su gobierno permitió más minería y deforestación en el Amazonas y debilitó las protecciones para los territorios indígenas.

**Qué pasó** – Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva fue reelegido presidente de Brasil en una segunda vuelta en octubre de 2022. Los líderes indígenas recibieron su victoria como una oportunidad para proteger sus tierras y derechos después de una campaña difícil donde su oponente, Flávio Bolsonaro, prometió detener el reconocimiento de nuevos territorios indígenas y aumentar la minería.

**Impacto** – El regreso de Lula ha ayudado a reconstruir el apoyo gubernamental para los pueblos indígenas. Su administración creó un Ministerio de los Pueblos Indígenas y fortaleció la agencia federal que protege las tierras indígenas. También anunciaron la tasa más baja de deforestación en el Amazonas desde 1988. Sin embargo, el nuevo Congreso tiene muchos legisladores que se oponen a los derechos territoriales indígenas y a las protecciones ambientales, lo que hace incierto el progreso.

**Próximo paso** – Los líderes indígenas dicen que deben mantenerse organizados y presionar al gobierno para que respete sus decisiones. Lula necesitará negociar cuidadosamente con un Congreso que podría resistirse a sus políticas ambientales e indígenas. Las comunidades indígenas también continúan trabajando para mejorar el acceso al voto y hacer oír sus voces en la democracia brasileña.

**Mensaje en una frase** – La reelección de Lula ofrece a los pueblos indígenas de Brasil una oportunidad vital para proteger sus tierras y derechos, pero el progreso real depende de superar los retos políticos que vienen.
